Title: Date Converter
Description: Convert Unix timestamps in seconds or milliseconds to ISO 8601, RFC 5322, UTC, local or custom-formatted dates and back, live in your browser.
Keywords: date converter, Unix timestamp, epoch converter, ISO 8601, RFC 2822, timestamp to date, date to timestamp, online date tool
CopyFailed: Could not copy to the clipboard. Select the text and copy it manually.
EmptyHint: Enter a Unix timestamp (seconds or milliseconds) or an ISO 8601 date.
Seo_Introduction: Turn a Unix timestamp into a readable date or a date string back into a timestamp. The converter recognises seconds, milliseconds and ISO 8601 automatically and outputs ISO, RFC 5322, UTC, your local time, a European format or your own pattern.
Seo_DetailedDescription:
In auto-detect mode a plain number with up to 11 integer digits is read as Unix seconds and a longer one as milliseconds; negative values (dates before 1970) and fractions are accepted. Anything else is parsed as a date string: ISO 8601 (`2024-02-29T12:00:00Z`), RFC 5322 (`Tue, 14 Nov 2023 22:13:20 GMT`) and other formats your browser's date parser understands. You can also force the input type to seconds, milliseconds or ISO 8601 — then hex or exponent notation such as `0x10` or `1e3` is rejected instead of being guessed.

Eight output formats are available: ISO 8601 in UTC with milliseconds, European `dd.MM.yyyy HH:mm:ss`, the UTC string, a local string written in the page language with your time zone, RFC 2822/5322 with a numeric `+0000` zone, Unix seconds, Unix milliseconds and a custom pattern built from `yyyy`, `MM`, `dd`, `HH`, `mm`, `ss` and `SSS`. The result updates as you type, and **Current Time (Now)** fills in the current moment.

Everything runs in JavaScript with the browser's own Date and Intl APIs; the values you paste are not sent anywhere. The supported range is that of JavaScript dates — about ±273,000 years around 1970; values outside it are reported as invalid.
Seo_Examples:
**Timestamp from a log**: `1700000000` (seconds) → ISO 8601 `2023-11-14T22:13:20.000Z`. The same moment in milliseconds, `1700000000000`, is detected automatically.

**Date to Unix time**: `2024-02-29T12:00:00Z` with the Unix Timestamp (Seconds) output gives `1709208000`.

**Before the epoch**: `-86400` → `1969-12-31T00:00:00.000Z`, exactly one day before 1 January 1970.

**Email header date**: `1700000000` with the RFC 2822 / 5322 output gives `Tue, 14 Nov 2023 22:13:20 +0000`.
Seo_HowToSteps:
### Step 1: Paste a value
Enter a Unix timestamp or a date string into **Date / Timestamp input**, or press **Current Time (Now)** to insert the current time.

### Step 2: Check the input type
Leave **Input Type** on **Auto-detect** or pick seconds, milliseconds or ISO 8601 explicitly when the value is ambiguous.

### Step 3: Choose the output
Select a format in **Output Format**; for **Custom Format**, type a pattern such as `yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm`.

### Step 4: Copy the result
The result updates automatically (**Convert** recalculates on demand); press **Copy** to copy it.
Seo_Tips:
- Milliseconds from before March 1973 have 11 digits or fewer and would be read as seconds in auto mode — select the milliseconds input type for them.
- An ISO string without a time zone (`2024-02-29T12:00`) is interpreted in your local time zone; add `Z` or an offset such as `+03:00` for UTC-safe input.
- ISO 8601, UTC and RFC outputs are always in UTC; European and custom formats use your browser's local time zone.
- In custom patterns `MM` is the month and `mm` the minutes; all other characters are copied literally.
- The local string follows the page language, so the same moment reads differently on the English and the Russian page.
